Men hvad end sprogets og samfundets oprindelse måtte være, kan det i det mindste sluttes, af den ringe omsorg, naturen har haft for at forene menneskeheden ved gensidige behov og lette brugen af tale, at hun har bidraget lidt til at gøre dem selskabelige og har lagt lidt af sit eget i alt, hvad de har gjort for at skabe sådanne bånd. Det er faktisk umuligt at fatte, hvorfor, i en naturtilstand, ét menneske skulle have mere brug for et andets hjælp, end en abe eller ulv behøver et andet af dens art. Eller, indrømmende at han gjorde, hvilke motiver kunne få den anden til at hjælpe ham? Eller selv da, ved hvilke midler kunne de blive enige om vilkårene? Jeg ved, det konstant gentages, at mennesket i en sådan tilstand ville have været det mest elendige af skabninger. Og hvis det faktisk er sandt, som jeg tror at have bevist, at han må have levet mange tidsaldre, før han kunne enten ønske eller have lejlighed til at undslippe den tilstand, ville dette kun være en anklage mod naturen og ikke mod det væsen, hun således ulykkeligt havde indrettet. Men som jeg forstår ordet elendig, har det enten slet ingen betydning eller betyder kun den smertefulde berøvelse af noget, eller en tilstand af lidelse i krop eller sjæl. Jeg ville være glad for at få forklaret, hvilken slags elendighed et frit væsen overhovedet kan lide, hvis hjerte er roligt, og hvis krop er sundt. Jeg ville også spørge, om et socialt eller et naturligt liv er mere tilbøjeligt til at blive uudholdeligt for dem, der nyder det. Vi ser omkring os næppe en skabning i det civile samfund, som ikke beklager sin eksistens; vi ser endda mange berøve sig selv så meget af den, som de kan, og menneskelige og guddommelige love tilsammen kan næppe standse uordenen. Har det nogensinde været kendt, at en vildmand i frihed satte sig i hovedet at klage over livet eller tage livet af sig selv? Lad os altså dømme, med mindre forfængelighed, på hvilken side den virkelige elendighed ligger. På den anden side kunne intet være mere ulykkeligt end vildmanden, blændet af videnskab, plaget af sine lidenskaber og ræsonnerende om en tilstand forskellig fra sin egen. Det forekommer, at Forsynet meget klogt arrangerede, at de evner, han potentielt besad, kun skulle udvikle sig, efterhånden som lejlighed bød sig til at udøve dem, så de ikke ville være overflødige eller byrdefulde for ham ved at vise sig før deres tid, ej heller langsomme og ubrugelige, når behovet for dem opstod. I instinktet alene havde han alt, hvad han behøvede for at leve i naturtilstanden; og med en udviklet forstand har han kun lige nok til at opretholde livet i samfundet.

Det forekommer ved første øjekast, at mennesker i en naturtilstand, der ikke har nogen moralske relationer eller bestemte forpligtelser indbyrdes, hverken kunne være gode eller dårlige, dydige eller lastefulde — medmindre vi tager disse termer i en fysisk betydning og kalder, hos et individ, de egenskaber laster, der kan skade hans bevarelse, og dyder dem, der bidrager til den; i hvilket tilfælde den mest dydige ville være den, der lagde mindst bånd på naturens rene impulser. Men uden at afvige fra ordenes almindelige betydning vil det være rigtigt at suspendere den dom, vi måtte være tilbøjelige til at danne om en sådan tilstand og at være på vagt mod vores fordomme, indtil vi har vejet sagen på upartiskhedens vægt og set, om dyder eller laster vejer tungest blandt civiliserede mennesker, og om deres dyder gør dem mere godt, end deres laster gør dem skade; indtil vi har opdaget, om videnskabernes fremgang i tilstrækkelig grad kompenserer dem for den skade, de gør hinanden, i samme grad som de bliver bedre informeret om det gode, de bør gøre; eller om de ikke samlet set ville være i en langt lykkeligere tilstand, hvis de intet havde at frygte eller håbe fra nogen, end som de er, underlagt almindelig afhængighed og tvunget til at tage alt fra dem, der forpligter sig til intet at give dem til gengæld.

Frem for alt, lad os ikke konkludere, sammen med Hobbes, at fordi mennesket ikke har nogen idé om godhed, må han være naturligt ondskabsfuld; at han er lastefuld, fordi han ikke kender dyd; at han altid nægter at gøre sine medskabninger tjenester, som han ikke mener, de har ret til at kræve; eller at han, i kraft af den ret, han med rette gør krav på til alt, hvad han har brug for, tåbeligt forestiller sig at være den eneste ejer af hele universet. Hobbes havde klart set fejlene ved alle de moderne definitioner af naturret. Men de konsekvenser, han udleder af sin egen, viser, at han forstår den i en lige så falsk betydning. Da han ræsonnerede ud fra de principper, han fastlægger, burde han have sagt, at naturtilstanden, da den er den, hvori omsorgen for vores egen bevarelse er mindst skadelig for andres, følgelig var bedst beregnet til at fremme fred og den mest passende for menneskeheden. Han siger det stik modsatte, fordi han uretmæssigt har inkluderet, som en del af vildmandens omsorg for sin selvopholdelse, tilfredsstillelsen af en mangfoldighed af lidenskaber, der er samfundets værk, og som har gjort love nødvendige. En ond mand, siger han, er et robust barn. Men det står tilbage at bevise, at mennesket i en naturtilstand er dette robuste barn; og selv hvis vi indrømmede, at han er det, hvad ville han slutte? Jo, sandelig, at hvis denne mand, når han er robust og stærk, var afhængig af andre, som han er, når han er svag, er der ingen udskejelse, han ikke ville være skyldig i: at han ville slå sin mor, når hun var for langsom til at give ham brystet; at han ville kvæle en af sine yngre brødre, hvis han fandt ham besværlig; eller at han ville bide en andens arm, hvis han forvoldte ham nogen ulejlighed. Men at mennesket i naturtilstanden er både stærk og afhængig involverer to modstridende antagelser. Mennesket er svagt, når det er afhængigt, og er sin egen herre, før det bliver stærkt. Hobbes reflekterede ikke over, at samme årsag, der forhindrer en vildmand i at gøre brug af sin fornuft (som vores jurister hævder), også forhindrer ham i at misbruge sine evner (som Hobbes selv indrømmer). Så det kan retfærdigt siges, at vildmænd ikke er onde, blot fordi de ikke ved, hvad det er at være god: for det er hverken forstandens udvikling eller lovens tøjle, der hindrer dem i at gøre ondt, men deres lidenskabers fredelige natur og deres uvidenhed om lasten — »så meget mere gavner uvidenhed om lasten den ene slags end kendskab til dyden den anden.« Der er et andet princip, der undslap Hobbes, som, idet det er skænket menneskeheden for at moderere, ved visse lejligheder, egoismens impetuositet, eller, før dens fødsel, ønsket om selvopholdelse, mildner den iver, hvormed han forfølger sit eget velfærd, ved en medfødt modvilje ved at se en medskabning lide. Jeg tror ikke, jeg behøver frygte modsigelse, når jeg fastholder, at mennesket er udstyret med den eneste naturlige dyd, som ikke engang den mest voldsomme nedrakker af menneskelig dyd kunne nægte ham. Jeg taler om medfølelse, en disposition, der passer skabninger så svage og udsat for så mange onder, som vi bestemt er — så meget mere universel og nyttig for menneskeheden, fordi den kommer før enhver form for refleksion, og samtidig så naturlig, at selv dyrene selv undertiden giver klare beviser på den. For ikke at nævne mødres ømhed over for deres unger og de farer, de udsætter sig for for at redde dem fra fare, er det velkendt, at heste er tilbageholdende med at træde på levende kroppe; intet dyr går nogensinde forbi liget af et andet af sin art; der er endda nogle, der giver deres artsfæller en slags begravelse; og kvægs sørgmodige rallen, når de går ind i slagtehuset, viser de indtryk, der gøres på dem af det forfærdelige skuespil, der møder dem. Vi finder, med fornøjelse, forfatteren til Biernes fabel tvunget til at indrømme, at mennesket er et medfølende og følsomt væsen, og, idet han lægger sin kolde, subtile stil til side, i det eksempel, han giver, præsenterer os for den patetiske beskrivelse af en mand, der, fra et indelukke, er tvunget til at se et vilddyr rive et barn fra dets mors arme, knuse dets sarte lemmer med sine morderiske tænder og rive dets dirrende indre i stykker med sine kløer. Hvilken rædselsfuld ophidselse må ikke øjenvidnet til en sådan scene opleve, selv om han ikke var personligt involveret! Hvilken ængstelse ville han ikke lide ved ikke at kunne give nogen hjælp til den besvimende mor og det døende spædbarn!

Sådan er den rene følelse af naturen, før al refleksion! Sådan er kraften af den naturlige medfølelse, som den største moralske fordærvelse hidtil næppe har været i stand til at ødelægge! For hver dag i vores teatre ser vi mænd bevæget — endda bragt til tårer — over en stakkels mands lidelser, som, hvis han var i tyrannens sted, sandsynligvis endda ville lægge til sine fjenders pinsler; som den blodtørstige Sulla, der var så følsom over for onder, han ikke havde forvoldt, eller hin Alexander af Pherae, der ikke turde gå hen og se nogen tragedie opført, af frygt for at blive set græde med Andromache og Priamos, selv om han kunne lytte uden at blive bevæget til skrigene fra alle de borgere, der dagligt blev kvalt på hans ordre.
»Naturen indrømmer, at hun gav menneskeslægten de blødeste hjerter, idet hun gav dem tårer.« (Juvenal, Satire xv, 151.)

Mandeville vidste vel, at trods al deres moral ville mennesker aldrig have været bedre end uhyrer, hvis naturen ikke havde skænket dem en følelse af medfølelse til at bistå deres fornuft. Men han så ikke, at af denne egenskab alene flyder alle de sociale dyder, han nægtede, at mennesket besad. For hvad er gavmildhed, mildhed eller menneskelighed, om ikke medfølelse anvendt på de svage, de skyldige eller på menneskeheden i almindelighed? Selv velvilje og venskab er, hvis vi dømmer rigtigt, kun virkninger af medfølelse, konstant rettet mod en bestemt genstand: for hvordan er det forskelligt at ønske, at en anden person ikke skal lide smerte og uro, og at ønske ham lykkelig? Selv om det var sandt, at medlidenhed ikke er mere end en følelse, der sætter os i den lidendes sted — en følelse, dunkel men levende hos en vildmand, udviklet, men svag hos det civiliserede menneske — ville denne sandhed ikke have anden konsekvens end at bekræfte min påstand. Medfølelsen må faktisk være stærkere, jo mere det dyr, der betragter en slags nød, identificerer sig med det dyr, der lider. Nu er det klart, at en sådan identifikation må have været langt mere fuldstændig i en naturtilstand end i en fornuftstilstand. Det er fornuften, der avler selvrespekten, og refleksionen, der bekræfter den. Det er fornuften, der vender det menneskelige sind tilbage på sig selv og skiller ham fra alt, hvad der kunne forstyrre eller plage ham. Det er filosofien, der isolerer ham og byder ham sige, ved synet af andres ulykke: »Omkom, om du vil, jeg er i sikkerhed.« Intet andet end sådanne almene onder, der truer hele samfundet, kan forstyrre filosoffens rolige søvn eller rive ham fra hans seng. Et mord kan begås under hans vindue uden følger; han skal blot lægge hænderne over ørerne og argumentere lidt med sig selv for at forhindre naturen, som er chokeret i ham, i at identificere sig med den ulykkelige lidende. Det uciviliserede menneske har ikke et sådant beundringsværdigt talent, og af mangel på fornuft og visdom er han altid tåbeligt parat til at adlyde menneskelighedens første impuls. Det er almuen, der stimler sammen ved optøjer og gadekampe, mens den vise mand klogt trækker sig. Det er pøblen og markedskonerne, der adskiller de stridende og forhindrer fine folk i at skære halsen over på hinanden.

Det er derfor sikkert, at medfølelse er en naturlig følelse, der, ved at moderere voldsomheden af kærligheden til selvet hos hvert enkelt individ, bidrager til hele artens bevarelse. Det er denne medfølelse, der uden refleksion skynder os til at lindre dem, der er i nød; det er denne, der i en naturtilstand træder i stedet for love, moral og dyder, med den fordel, at ingen fristes til at adlyde dens milde stemme. Det er denne, der altid vil forhindre en stærk vildmand i at berøve et svagt barn eller en svag gammel mand det underhold, de måtte have erhvervet med smerte og besvær, så længe han ser en mulighed for at sørge for sig selv ad andre veje. Det er denne, der i stedet for at indprente den ophøjede maksime om rationel retfærdighed, »Gør mod andre, som du vil, de skal gøre mod dig,« indgiver alle mennesker den anden maksime om naturlig godhed — langt mindre fuldkommen, men måske mere nyttig: »Gør godt mod dig selv med så lidt skade som muligt mod andre.« Kort sagt, det er i denne naturlige følelse snarere end i nogen subtile argumenter, vi må søge årsagen til den modvilje, ethvert menneske ville føle ved at gøre ondt, selv uafhængigt af opdragelsens maksimer. Selv om det måtte tilhøre Sokrates og andre sind af samme håndværk at erhverve dyd ved fornuft, ville den menneskelige slægt for længst være ophørt med at eksistere, hvis dens bevarelse kun havde afhængt af ræsonnementerne hos de individer, der udgjorde den.

Med lidenskaber så lidt aktive, og en så god tøjle på dem, var mænd, der var mere vilde end onde og mere ude på at vogte sig selv mod den skade, der kunne gøres mod dem, end på at gøre skade mod andre, på ingen måde udsat for meget farlige uoverensstemmelser. De havde ingen omgang med hinanden og var derfor fremmede for forfængelighed, ærbødighed, agtelse og foragt. De havde ikke den mindste idé om mit og dit og ingen sand forestilling om retfærdighed. De så på enhver vold, de blev udsat for, snarere som en skade, der let kunne repareres, end som en forbrydelse, der fortjente straf, og de tænkte aldrig på at tage hævn undtagen måske mekanisk og på stedet, ligesom en hund undertiden vil bide den sten, der kastes på den. Deres skænderier ville derfor sjældent have meget blodige følger, da emnet for dem blot ville være et spørgsmål om underhold. Men jeg er opmærksom på en større fare, der står tilbage at bemærke.

Blandt de lidenskaber, der rører det menneskelige hjerte, er der en, der gør kønnene nødvendige for hinanden, og som er yderst glødende og impetuøs — en frygtelig lidenskab, der trodser fare, overvinder alle hindringer og i sine udfald synes designet til at bringe ødelæggelse over selve den menneskelige slægt, den faktisk er ment at bevare. Hvad må der blive af mænd, der er overladt til denne brutale og grænseløse vrede, uden blufærdighed, uden skam, og som dagligt forsvarer deres elskov til prisen af deres blod?

Det må først og fremmest indrømmes, at jo mere voldsomme lidenskaberne er, jo mere nødvendige bliver love for at holde dem i skak. Men sat til side lovenes utilstrækkelighed til at opnå dette formål — hvilket fremgår klart af de forbrydelser og uordener, disse lidenskaber dagligt giver anledning til blandt os — bør vi godt undersøge, om disse onder ikke opstod sammen med selve lovene. For i så fald, selv hvis lovene var i stand til at undertrykke sådanne onder, ville det mindste, der kunne forventes af dem, være at standse en skadelighed, der ikke ville være opstået uden dem.

Lad os begynde med at skelne de fysiske og moralske ingredienser i kærlighedens følelse. Den fysiske del af kærligheden er det almene begær, der driver kønnene til at forene sig med hinanden. Den moralske del er det, der bestemmer og fæster dette begær udelukkende på én bestemt genstand, eller i det mindste giver det en større grad af energi mod den således foretrukne genstand. Det er let at se, at den moralske del af kærligheden er en kunstig følelse, født af social skik og forstærket af kvinder med megen omhu og snildhed for at etablere deres imperium og sætte i magt det køn, der burde adlyde. Denne følelse, der hviler på visse idéer om skønhed og fortjeneste, som en vildmand ikke er i stand til at erhverve, og på sammenligninger, han ikke er i stand til at lave, må for ham være næsten ikke-eksisterende. For da hans sind ikke kan danne abstrakte idéer om proportion og regelmæssighed, er hans hjerte ikke modtageligt for følelserne af kærlighed og beundring, der umærkeligt frembringes ved anvendelsen af disse idéer. Han følger udelukkende den karakter, naturen har indplantet i ham, og ikke smage, han aldrig kunne have erhvervet, så enhver kvinde lige så godt opfylder hans formål.

Mænd i en naturtilstand, indskrænket blot til det fysiske i kærligheden, og heldige nok til at være uvidende om de forfinelser, der hvæsser appetitten og samtidig øger vanskeligheden ved at tilfredsstille den, må være underlagt færre og mindre voldsomme lidenskabsanfald og dermed falde i færre og mindre voldsomme stridigheder. Fantasien, der forårsager sådanne ødelæggelser blandt os, taler aldrig til vildmændenes hjerte, der roligt afventer naturens impulser, giver efter for dem ufrivilligt, med mere fornøjelse end glød, og, deres behov en gang tilfredsstillet, mister begæret. Det er derfor uomtvisteligt, at kærligheden, ligesom alle andre lidenskaber, må have erhvervet sig i samfundet den glødende impetuositet, der gør den så ofte fatal for menneskeheden. Og det er endnu mere absurd at fremstille vildmænd som konstant skærende halsen over på hinanden for at forkæle deres brutalitet, fordi denne mening er direkte i modstrid med erfaringen. Caraiberne, der hidtil har afveget mindst af alle fra naturtilstanden, er faktisk de fredeligste folk i deres elskov og de mindst udsat for jalousi, selv om de lever i et varmt klima, der altid synes at tænde lidenskaberne.

Hvad angår de slutninger, der måtte drages af tilfældet med flere dyrearter, hvis hanner fylder vores hønsegårde med blod og slagteri eller om foråret får skovene til at give genlyd af deres skænderier om hunnerne, må vi begynde med at udelukke alle de arter, hvor naturen tydeligt har etableret, i de to køns sammenlignelige magt, relationer forskellige fra dem, der eksisterer blandt os. Således kan vi ikke basere nogen konklusion om mænd på kamphanernes vaner. I de arter, hvor proportionen er bedre overholdt, må disse kampe udelukkende skyldes hunnernes knaphed sammenlignet med hannerne — eller, hvad der kommer ud på det samme, de intervaller, hvor hunnen konsekvent afviser hannens tilnærmelser. For hvis hver hun kun tillader hannen i to måneder om året, er det det samme, som hvis antallet af hunner var fem sjettedele mindre. Nu gælder ingen af disse to tilfælde for den menneskelige art, hvor antallet af hunner sædvanligvis overstiger antallet af hanner, og hvor det aldrig er blevet observeret, selv blandt vildmænd, at hunnerne, som hos andre dyr, har deres faste tider for lidenskab og ligegyldighed. Desuden tænder individerne i flere af disse arter alle på én gang, og der kommer et frygteligt øjeblik af universel lidenskab, tumult og uorden blandt dem — en scene, der aldrig ses i den menneskelige art, hvis kærlighed ikke er sæsonbestemt. Så vi må ikke konkludere, fra disse dyrs kampe om nydelsen af hunnerne, at det samme ville være tilfældet med menneskeheden i en naturtilstand. Og selv hvis vi drog en sådan konklusion, ser vi, at sådanne stridigheder ikke udrydder andre slags dyr, og vi har ingen grund til at tro, at de ville være mere fatale for vores. Det er faktisk klart, at de ville gøre endnu mindre skade end er tilfældet i en samfundstilstand — især i de lande, hvor moralen stadig holdes i nogen ære, og elskeres jalousi og ægtemænds hævn dagligt forårsager dueller, mord og endnu værre forbrydelser, hvor forpligtelsen til evig troskab kun frembringer ægteskabsbrud, og selve lovene om ære og afholdenhed nødvendigvis øger udsvævelser og mangedobler aborter.

Lad os altså konkludere, at mennesket i en naturtilstand, vandrende op og ned gennem skovene, uden industri, uden tale og uden hjem, lige fremmed for krig og for alle bånd, hverken behøvende sine medskabninger eller ønskende at gøre dem fortræd, og måske ikke engang skelnende dem fra hinanden — lad os konkludere, at, idet han var selvtilstrækkelig og underlagt så få lidenskaber, kunne han ikke have andre følelser eller anden viden end den, der passede til hans situation; at han kun følte sine faktiske behov og tilsidesatte alt, hvad han ikke mente sig umiddelbart berørt af, og at hans forstand ikke gjorde større fremskridt end hans forfængelighed. Hvis han ved et tilfælde gjorde en opdagelse, var han desto mindre i stand til at meddele den til andre, eftersom han ikke engang kendte sine egne børn. Enhver kunst ville nødvendigvis omkomme med sin opfinder, hvor der ikke var nogen slags uddannelse blandt mennesker, og generationer fulgte generationer uden den mindste fremgang. Idet alle satte ud fra samme punkt, må århundreder være forløbet i de tidligste tidsaldres barbari; da slægten allerede var gammel, forblev mennesket et barn.

Hvis jeg har dvælet så længe ved denne formodede primitive tilstand, er det, fordi jeg havde så mange gamle fejl og dybt rodfæstede fordomme at rykke op med rode, og derfor anså det for min pligt at grave ned til deres rødder og ved hjælp af et sandt billede af naturtilstanden vise, hvor langt selv menneskehedens naturlige uligheder er fra at have den realitet og indflydelse, moderne skribenter antager.

Det er faktisk let at se, at mange af de forskelle, der skiller mennesker fra hinanden, blot er virkningen af vane og af de forskellige livsformer, folk antager i samfundet. Således er en robust eller sart konstitution, og den styrke eller svaghed, den medfører, oftere virkningen af en hærdet eller blødagtig opdragelse end af kroppens oprindelige udrustning. Det samme gælder sindets kræfter: opdragelsen gør ikke blot en forskel mellem dem, der er dannede, og dem, der ikke er det, men forøger endda de forskelle, der eksisterer blandt de første, i forhold til deres respektive grader af dannelse — ligesom afstanden mellem en kæmpe og en dværg på samme vej øges med hvert skridt, de tager. Hvis vi sammenligner den uhyrlige mangfoldighed i opdragelsen og levevisen hos de forskellige klasser af mennesker i samfundstilstanden med ensartetheden og enkelheden af det dyriske og vilde liv, hvor alle lever af samme slags føde og på nøjagtig samme måde og gør nøjagtig samme ting, er det let at fatte, hvor meget mindre forskellen mellem menneske og menneske må være i en naturtilstand end i en samfundstilstand, og hvor stærkt menneskehedens naturlige ulighed må forstørres af de sociale institutioners uligheder.

Men selv hvis naturen virkelig udviste, i fordelingen af sine gaver, den partiskhed, der tilskrives hende, hvilken fordel ville den største af hendes yndlinge drage af det, til skade for andre, i en tilstand, der knap nok tillader nogen slags relation mellem dem? Hvor der ikke er nogen kærlighed, hvad nytte gør skønheden? Hvad nytte gør vid for dem, der ikke samtaler, eller list for dem, der ikke har noget at gøre med andre? Jeg hører det konstant gentaget, at i en sådan tilstand ville den stærke undertrykke den svage. Men hvad menes der her med undertrykkelse? Nogle, siges det, ville voldsomt herske over andre, der ville sukke under en slavisk underkastelse for deres luner. Dette er ganske vist nøjagtigt, hvad jeg ser være tilfældet blandt os, men jeg ser ikke, hvordan det kan udledes om mennesker i en naturtilstand, der ikke let kunne bringes til at fatte, hvad vi mener med herredømme og trældom. En mand kunne ganske vist gribe de frugter, en anden havde samlet, det vildt, han havde dræbt, eller den hule, han havde valgt som ly. Men hvordan ville han nogensinde kunne kræve lydighed? Og hvilke bånd af afhængighed kunne der være blandt mænd uden ejendele? Hvis jeg for eksempel jages væk fra et træ, kan jeg gå til det næste; hvis jeg forstyrres et sted, hvad hindrer mig i at gå et andet sted hen? Igen, hvis jeg tilfældigvis skulle møde en mand så meget stærkere end mig selv, og samtidig så fordærvet, så doven og så barbarisk, at han tvinger mig til at sørge for hans underhold, mens han selv forbliver i lediggang, ville han skulle passe på aldrig at tage øjnene fra mig et øjeblik; han ville skulle binde mig fast, før han gik i seng, eller jeg ville helt sikkert enten knuse hans hoved eller flygte. Det vil sige, han ville frivilligt skulle udsætte sig for langt større besvær, end han søger at undgå, eller kunne give mig. Efter alt det, lad ham være uagtsom blot et øjeblik, lad ham blot dreje hovedet til siden ved en pludselig lyd, og jeg vil være tyve skridt væk på et øjeblik, fortabt i skoven; mine lænker brækket, ville han aldrig se mig igen.

Uden at spilde mere tid på disse detaljer, må enhver se, at da trældommens bånd kun dannes af menneskenes gensidige afhængighed af hinanden og af de gensidige behov, der forener dem, er det umuligt at gøre nogen mand til slave, medmindre han først er bragt i en situation, hvor han ikke kan undvære andres hjælp. Og da en sådan situation ikke eksisterer i en naturtilstand, er enhver der sin egen herre, og den stærkestes lov har ingen virkning.

Efter at have bevist, at menneskehedens ulighed næppe mærkes, og at dens indflydelse er næsten ingen i en naturtilstand, må jeg derefter vise dens oprindelse og spore dens fremgang gennem den menneskelige ånds successive udviklinger. Efter at have vist, at menneskelig perfektibilitet, de sociale dyder og de øvrige evner, det naturlige menneske potentielt besad, aldrig kunne udvikle sig af sig selv, men måtte kræve det tilfældige sammenløb af mange fremmede årsager, der måske aldrig ville opstå, og uden hvilke han ville være forblevet for evigt i sin oprindelige tilstand, må jeg nu samle og overveje de forskellige tilfældigheder, der måske har forbedret den menneskelige forstand, mens de fordærvede arten, og gjort mennesket ondt, mens de gjorde ham selskabelig — så at bringe ham og verden fra hin fjerne periode til det punkt, hvor vi nu betragter dem.

Jeg indrømmer, at, da de begivenheder, jeg vil beskrive, kunne være sket på forskellige måder, har jeg intet at bestemme mit valg ved undtagen formodninger. Men sådanne formodninger bliver grunde, når de er de mest sandsynlige, der kan drages af tingenes natur, og det eneste middel til at opdage sandheden. De konsekvenser, jeg vil udlede, vil dog ikke være blot formodede, for ud fra de principper, der lige er fremlagt, ville det være umuligt at danne nogen anden teori, der ikke ville give de samme resultater, og hvoraf jeg ikke kunne drage de samme konklusioner.

Dette vil være en tilstrækkelig undskyldning for, at jeg ikke dvæler ved, hvordan tidens gang opvejer den ringe sandsynlighed af begivenhederne; ved den overraskende kraft af trivielle årsager, når deres virkning er vedvarende; ved umuligheden, på den ene side, af at ødelægge visse hypoteser, selv om vi på den anden side ikke kan give dem den sikkerhed, kendte kendsgerninger har; ved at det ligger inden for historiens område, når to kendsgerninger gives som virkelige og skal forbindes ved en række mellemliggende kendsgerninger, der er ukendte eller antages at være det, at levere sådanne kendsgerninger, der måtte forbinde dem; og ved at det ligger inden for filosofiens område, når historien er tavs, at bestemme lignende kendsgerninger, der tjener samme formål; og endelig ved indflydelsen af lighed, som, i tilfælde af begivenheder, reducerer kendsgerningerne til et meget mindre antal forskellige klasser, end almindeligt forestilles. Det er nok for mig at fremlægge disse vink til mine dommeres overvejelse og at have arrangeret det sådan, at den almindelige læser slet ikke behøver at overveje dem.

chapters.title: Part II
paragraphs: The first man who, having enclosed a piece of ground, took it into his head to say This is mine, and found people simple enough to believe him, was the true founder of civil society. How many crimes, wars, and murders, how many horrors and misfortunes might mankind have been spared if someone had pulled up the stakes, or filled in the ditch, and shouted to his fellows, "Beware of listening to this impostor; you are ruined if you forget that the fruits of the earth belong to all and the earth itself to no one." But it is very likely that things had by then already reached a point where they could no longer continue as they were, since the idea of property depends on many prior ideas that could only have been acquired gradually and cannot have formed all at once in the human mind.

Mankind must have made considerable progress, acquired considerable knowledge and skill, and transmitted and increased them from one age to the next, before arriving at this last stage of the state of nature. Let us, then, go further back and try to bring together under a single viewpoint that slow succession of events and discoveries in their most natural order.

Man's first feeling was that of his own existence, and his first care that of self-preservation. The produce of the earth furnished him with all he needed, and instinct told him how to use it. Hunger and other appetites made him experience, at various times, various ways of being; and among these was one that pushed him to propagate his species—a blind impulse that, having nothing to do with the heart, produced a merely animal act. Once the need was satisfied, the two sexes no longer recognized each other; and even the child was nothing to its mother as soon as it could do without her.

Such was the condition of infant man: the life of an animal, limited at first to mere sensations, hardly profiting from the gifts nature bestowed on him, much less capable of entertaining the thought of forcing anything from her. But difficulties soon presented themselves, and it became necessary to learn to overcome them. The height of the trees, which prevented him from gathering their fruits; the competition of other animals desiring the same fruits; and the ferocity of those who needed them for their own preservation—all this obliged him to apply himself to physical exercises. He had to become active, swift of foot, and vigorous in the fight. Natural weapons—stones and sticks—were easily found. He learned to overcome nature's obstacles, to fight when necessary with other animals, and to dispute the means of subsistence even with other men, or to make up for what he was forced to give up to a stronger one.

As the human race grew more numerous, men's cares increased. The difference of soils, climates, and seasons must have introduced some differences in their ways of living. Barren years, long and harsh winters, and scorching summers that parched the fruits of the earth must have demanded a new kind of industry. On the seashore and the banks of rivers, they invented the hook and line, and became fishermen and eaters of fish. In the forests they made bows and arrows, and became hunters and warriors. In cold countries they clothed themselves with the skins of the beasts they had slain. Lightning, a volcano, or some lucky chance acquainted them with fire, a new resource against the rigors of winter. They next learned how to preserve this element, then how to reproduce it, and finally how to prepare with it the flesh of animals they had previously eaten raw.

This repeated relation of various beings to himself, and of beings to one another, would naturally give rise in the human mind to the perception of certain relations between them. Thus the relations we denote by the words great, small, strong, weak, swift, slow, fearful, bold, and the like, compared almost insensibly when need arose, must have at length produced in him a kind of reflection, or rather a mechanical prudence, that would point out to him the precautions most necessary for his security.

The new intelligence that resulted from this development increased his superiority over other animals by making him conscious of it. From now on he would try to ensnare them, play them a thousand tricks, and, though many of them might surpass him in speed or strength, would in time become master of some and the scourge of others. Thus, the first time he looked into himself, he felt the first stirring of pride; and, at a time when he hardly knew how to distinguish the different orders of beings, by looking on his species as the highest, he prepared the way for claiming pre-eminence as an individual.

Other men, it is true, were not then to him what they are now to us, and he had no greater dealings with them than with other animals; yet they were not left out of his observations. The conformities he would in time discover between them, and between himself and his female, led him to judge of others not yet perceptible. Finding that they all behaved as he himself would have done in like circumstances, he naturally inferred that their manner of thinking and acting was entirely in conformity with his own. This important truth, once deeply impressed on his mind, must have induced him, by an intuitive feeling more certain and far quicker than any kind of reasoning, to follow the rules of conduct he had best observe toward them for his own security and advantage.

Taught by experience that the love of well-being is the sole motive of human actions, he found himself in a position to distinguish the few cases in which mutual interest might justify him in relying on the help of his fellows, and also the still fewer cases in which a conflict of interests might give him reason to suspect them. In the first case, he joined them in the same herd, or at most in some kind of loose association that laid no restraint on its members and lasted no longer than the brief occasion that had formed it. In the second case, each one sought his own private advantage—either by open force, if he thought himself strong enough, or by address and cunning, if he felt himself the weaker.

In this way men may have imperceptibly acquired some rough ideas of mutual undertakings and of the advantages of fulfilling them—but only so far as their present and apparent interest was concerned, since they were utter strangers to foresight and were so far from worrying about the distant future that they hardly thought of tomorrow. If a deer was to be taken, every one of them saw that to succeed he had to stay faithfully at his post; but if a hare happened to come within reach of any one of them, there is no doubt he would pursue it without scruple, and, having seized his prey, would care very little if by doing so he made his companions miss theirs.

It is easy to understand that such dealings would not require a language much more refined than that of crows or monkeys, which associate together for much the same purpose. Inarticulate cries, plenty of gestures, and some imitative sounds must have been for a long time the universal language; and by the addition, in every country, of some conventional articulate sounds—of which, as I have already hinted, the first institution is not easy to explain—particular languages were produced. But these were rough and imperfect, and much like those still found today among certain savage nations.

Hurried on by the rush of time, by the abundance of things I have to say, and by the almost imperceptible progress of things in their beginnings, I pass over in an instant a multitude of ages; for the slower the events were in their succession, the more rapidly they may be described.

These first advances enabled men to make others more rapidly. As they grew more enlightened, they grew more industrious. They stopped falling asleep under the first tree or in the first cave that offered them shelter; they invented several kinds of implements out of hard, sharp stones, which they used to dig the earth and cut wood. They then made huts out of branches, and afterward learned to plaster them with mud and clay. This was the epoch of a first revolution, which established and distinguished families and introduced a kind of property—itself the source of a thousand quarrels and conflicts. Since the strongest were probably the first to build themselves huts they felt able to defend, it may be concluded that the weak found it much easier and safer to imitate them than to try to dislodge them. And among those already provided with huts, no one could have any incentive to take possession of his neighbor's—not so much because it didn't belong to him as because it could be of no use to him, and he could not seize it without exposing himself to a desperate battle with the family that occupied it.

The first expansions of the human heart were the effect of a new situation, which united husbands and wives, parents and children, under one roof. The habit of living together soon gave rise to the finest feelings humanity has known: conjugal love and parental affection. Every family became a little society, all the more united because liberty and mutual attachment were the only bonds of its union. The sexes, whose way of life had until then been the same, began now to adopt different ways of living. The women became more sedentary and grew accustomed to tending the hut and their children, while the men went abroad in search of their common subsistence. From living a softer life, both sexes also began to lose something of their strength and ferocity. But while individuals became to some extent less able to face wild beasts on their own, they found it, on the other hand, easier to assemble and resist in common.

The simplicity and solitude of man's life in this new condition, the fewness of his needs, and the tools he had invented to satisfy them, left him a great deal of leisure, which he used to provide himself with many conveniences unknown to his ancestors. This was the first yoke he unwittingly imposed on himself, and the first source of the evils he prepared for his descendants. For besides continuing in this way to weaken both body and mind, these conveniences lost with use almost all their power to please, and even degenerated into real needs, until going without them became far more disagreeable than possessing them had ever been pleasant. People would have been unhappy at losing them, even though possessing them had not made them happy.

Here we can see a little better how the use of speech became established and was insensibly improved within each family; and we may also form a conjecture about how various causes may have extended and accelerated the progress of language by making it more and more necessary. Floods or earthquakes surrounded inhabited areas with precipices or water; revolutions of the globe tore portions off the continent and made them islands. It is easy to see that, among men thus gathered together and compelled to live together, a common idiom must have arisen much more easily than among those still wandering through the forests of the continent. Thus it is very possible that, after their first essays in navigation, the islanders brought over the use of speech to the continent; and it is at least very probable that communities and languages were first established on islands, and even perfected there before they were known on the mainland.

Everything now begins to change. Men, who up to now had been roaming the woods, by taking to a more settled way of life, came gradually together, formed separate bodies, and at length in every country a distinct nation arose, united in character and manners not by regulations or laws but by uniformity of life and food and the common influence of climate. Permanent neighborhood could not fail to produce, in time, some connection between different families. Among young people of opposite sexes living in neighboring huts, the transient relation required by nature soon led, through mutual exchanges, to another sort of relation no less agreeable and more lasting. Men began now to take account of the differences between objects and to make comparisons; they imperceptibly acquired the ideas of beauty and merit, which soon gave rise to feelings of preference. From seeing each other often, they could no longer do without seeing each other constantly. A tender and pleasant feeling slipped into their souls, and the least opposition turned it into impetuous fury: with love arose jealousy; discord triumphed; and human blood was sacrificed to the gentlest of all passions.

As ideas and feelings succeeded one another, and heart and mind were brought into play, men continued to lay aside their original wildness. Their private connections grew more intimate every day as their boundaries extended. They got into the habit of gathering before their huts around a large tree; singing and dancing—the true offspring of love and leisure—became the amusement, or rather the occupation, of men and women thus assembled together with nothing else to do. Each one began to look at the rest, and to want to be looked at in turn; and so a value came to be attached to public esteem. Whoever sang or danced best, whoever was the handsomest, the strongest, the most skillful, or the most eloquent, came to be the most regarded. This was the first step toward inequality and, at the same time, toward vice. From these first distinctions arose, on the one hand, vanity and contempt, and on the other, shame and envy; and the fermentation caused by these new yeasts ended in producing combinations fatal to innocence and happiness.

As soon as men began to value one another and the idea of social consideration had taken root in the mind, every one staked his claim to it, and it became impossible to refuse it to anyone with impunity. From this arose the first obligations of civility even among savages, and every intended injury became an affront, because besides the harm that might result from it, the injured party was certain to find in it a contempt for his person, which was often more unbearable than the harm itself.

Thus, as every man punished the contempt shown him by others, in proportion to his opinion of himself, revenge became terrible, and men bloody and cruel. This is precisely the state reached by most of the savage nations known to us. And it is for want of having made a proper distinction in our ideas, and seen how very far they already are from the state of nature, that so many writers have hastily concluded that man is naturally cruel and requires civil institutions to make him milder. Whereas nothing is gentler than man in his primitive state, since he is placed by nature at an equal distance from the stupidity of brutes and the fatal ingenuity of civilized man. Equally confined by instinct and reason to the sole care of guarding himself against the mischiefs that threaten him, he is restrained by natural compassion from doing any harm to others, and is not led to do such a thing even in return for injuries received. For, according to the wise Locke's axiom, "There can be no injury where there is no property."

But it must be noted that the society thus formed, and the relations thus established among men, demanded of them qualities different from those they possessed in their primitive constitution. Morality began to appear in human actions, and every one, before the institution of law, was the only judge and avenger of the injuries done him; so the goodness that was suitable in the pure state of nature was no longer proper in the newborn state of society. Punishments had to be made more severe as opportunities of offending became more frequent, and the dread of vengeance had to take the place of the rigor of the law. So although men had become less patient, and their natural compassion had already suffered some diminution, this period of expansion of the human faculties—keeping a just mean between the indolence of the primitive state and the petulant activity of our egoism—must have been the happiest and most stable of epochs. The more we reflect on it, the more we shall find that this state was the least subject to revolutions, and altogether the very best man could experience; so that he can only have departed from it through some fatal accident, which, for the public good, should never have happened. The example of savages, most of whom have been found in this state, seems to confirm that mankind was meant to remain in it, that this is the real youth of the world, and that all subsequent advances have been, in appearance, so many steps toward the perfection of the individual, but in reality toward the decrepitude of the species.

So long as men were content with their rustic huts; so long as they were satisfied with clothes made of animal skins sewn together with thorns and fishbones, adorned themselves only with feathers and shells, and continued to paint their bodies different colors, to improve and beautify their bows and arrows, and to make with sharp stones fishing boats or clumsy musical instruments; in a word, so long as they undertook only what a single person could accomplish, and confined themselves to such arts as did not require the joint labor of several hands, they lived free, healthy, honest, and happy lives, so long as their nature allowed, and continued to enjoy the pleasures of mutual and independent dealings. But from the moment one man began to need the help of another, from the moment it appeared advantageous for one man to have provisions enough for two, equality disappeared, property was introduced, work became indispensable, and vast forests turned into smiling fields that man had to water with the sweat of his brow, where slavery and misery were soon seen to sprout and grow with the crops.

Metallurgy and agriculture were the two arts that produced this great revolution. The poets tell us it was gold and silver, but for the philosophers it was iron and grain that first civilized men, and ruined humanity. Thus both were unknown to the savages of America, who for that very reason are still savage. Other nations also seem to have remained in a state of barbarism while they practiced only one of these arts. One of the best reasons, perhaps, why Europe has been, if not longer, at least more consistently and highly civilized than the rest of the world, is that it is at once the most abundant in iron and the most fertile in grain.

It is difficult to conjecture how men first came to know and use iron, since it is impossible to suppose they would of themselves think of digging the ore out of the mine and preparing it for smelting before they knew what would result. On the other hand, we have all the less reason to suppose this discovery the effect of any accidental fire, since mines are formed only in barren places, bare of trees and plants—so it looks as if nature had taken pains to hide the fatal secret from us. There remains, therefore, only the extraordinary accident of some volcano which, by ejecting metallic substances already in fusion, would have suggested to the spectators the idea of imitating this natural operation. And we must further conceive them as possessed of uncommon courage and foresight to undertake so laborious a task, with so distant a prospect of profiting by it—qualities only found together in minds more advanced than we can suppose those of these first discoverers to have been.

As for agriculture, its principles were known long before they were put into practice; and it is indeed hardly possible that men, constantly employed in drawing their subsistence from plants and trees, should not readily acquire some knowledge of the means used by nature for the propagation of vegetables. In all probability, however, it was very long before their industry took that turn—whether because trees, which together with hunting and fishing supplied them with food, did not require their attention; or because they were ignorant of the use of grain, or lacked tools to cultivate it; or because they lacked foresight regarding future needs; or, lastly, because they had no means of preventing others from robbing them of the fruits of their labor.

When they became more industrious, it is natural to believe that they began, with the help of sharp stones and pointed sticks, to cultivate a few vegetables or roots around their huts. But it was long before they knew how to prepare grain, or were provided with the implements necessary for raising it in any large quantity—not to mention how essential it is to husbandry to consent to immediate loss in order to reap a future gain, a precaution very foreign to the cast of a savage's mind, since, as I have said, he hardly foresees in the morning what he will need at night.

The invention of the other arts must therefore have been necessary to compel mankind to apply themselves to agriculture. No sooner were craftsmen needed to smelt and forge iron than others were needed to maintain them. The more hands that were employed in manufactures, the fewer were left to provide for the common subsistence, even though the number of mouths to be fed remained the same. And as some required commodities in exchange for their iron, the rest at length discovered the method of making iron serve to multiply commodities. By this means, the arts of husbandry and agriculture were established on the one hand, and the art of working metals and multiplying their uses on the other.

The cultivation of the earth necessarily brought about its distribution; and property, once recognized, gave rise to the first rules of justice. For to secure to each man his own, each had to have something. Besides, as men began to look forward to the future, and all had something to lose, every one had reason to fear that reprisals would follow any injury he might do to another. This origin is all the more natural because it is impossible to conceive how property could come from anything but manual labor: for what else can a man add to things he did not originally create, so as to make them his property? It is the husbandman's labor alone that, by giving him a title to the produce of the ground he has tilled, gives him a claim also to the land itself, at least until harvest; and so, year after year, a continuous possession is easily transformed into property. When the ancients, says Grotius, gave Ceres the title of Legislatrix, and to a festival celebrated in her honor the name of Thesmophoria, they meant by this that the distribution of lands had produced a new kind of right—that is, the right of property, which is different from the right deducible from the law of nature.

In this state of affairs, equality might have been maintained had the talents of individuals been equal, and had, for example, the use of iron and the consumption of commodities always exactly balanced each other. But since there was nothing to preserve this balance, it was soon disturbed. The strongest did the most work; the most skillful turned his labor to the best account; the most ingenious devised ways of reducing his labor. The husbandman wanted more iron, or the smith more grain, and while both labored equally, the one gained a great deal by his work, while the other could hardly support himself. Thus natural inequality unfolds itself imperceptibly along with that of combination, and the difference between men, developed by their different circumstances, becomes more perceptible and permanent in its effects, and begins, in the same proportion, to influence the lot of individuals.

Matters once at this pitch, it is easy to imagine the rest. I will not detain the reader with a description of the successive invention of other arts, the development of language, the trial and use of talents, the inequality of fortunes, the use and abuse of riches, and all the details connected with them which the reader can easily supply for himself. I will confine myself to a glance at mankind in this new situation.

Behold, then, all human faculties developed, memory and imagination in full play, egoism interested, reason active, and the mind almost at the highest point of its perfection. Behold all the natural qualities in action: the rank and condition of every man assigned him; not only his share of property and his power to serve or injure others, but also his wit, beauty, strength or skill, merit or talents. And these being the only qualities capable of commanding respect, it soon became necessary to possess them or to pretend to.

It now became the interest of men to appear what they really were not. To be and to seem became two totally different things; and from this distinction sprang insolent pomp and cheating trickery, with all the numerous vices that go in their train. On the other hand, free and independent as men had been before, they were now, in consequence of a multitude of new wants, brought into subjection, as it were, to all nature, and especially to one another. Each became in some degree a slave even in becoming the master of other men. If rich, they needed others' services; if poor, others' help; and even a middling condition did not enable them to do without one another. Man must now, therefore, have been perpetually employed in getting others to interest themselves in his lot, and in making them, apparently at least if not really, find their advantage in promoting his own. He must therefore have been sly and artful in his behavior to some, and imperious and cruel to others, being under a kind of necessity to ill-use all the people he needed when he could not frighten them into compliance and did not judge it his interest to be useful to them. Insatiable ambition, the thirst to raise their respective fortunes—not so much out of real need as from the desire to outdo others—inspired all men with a vile inclination to harm one another, and with a secret jealousy which is all the more dangerous because it puts on the mask of benevolence to carry its point with greater security. In short, there arose rivalry and competition on the one hand, and conflicting interests on the other, together with a secret desire on both sides to profit at the expense of others. All these evils were the first effects of property, and the inseparable attendants of growing inequality.

Before the invention of signs to represent riches, wealth could hardly consist in anything but lands and cattle—the only real possessions men can have. But when inheritances increased in number and extent until they covered the whole of the land and bordered on one another, one man could only enlarge himself at another's expense. At the same time, the supernumeraries, who had been too weak or too lazy to make such acquisitions, and had grown poor without sustaining any loss—because while they saw everything change around them, they themselves remained the same—were obliged to receive their subsistence, or steal it, from the rich. And this soon bred, according to their different characters, either dominion and slavery, or violence and pillage. The wealthy, for their part, had no sooner begun to taste the pleasure of command than they disdained all others; and, using their old slaves to acquire new ones, they thought of nothing but subduing and enslaving their neighbors, like ravenous wolves which, having once tasted human flesh, despise every other food and from then on seek only men to devour.

Thus, as the most powerful or the most miserable considered their might or their misery as a kind of right to the possessions of others, equivalent in their view to that of property, the destruction of equality was attended by the most terrible disorders. Usurpations by the rich, robbery by the poor, and the unbridled passions of both, suppressed the cries of natural compassion and the still feeble voice of justice, and filled men with avarice, ambition, and vice. Between the title of the strongest and that of the first occupier, there arose perpetual conflicts that never ended but in battles and bloodshed. The newborn state of society thus gave rise to a horrible state of war; men, thus harassed and corrupted, were no longer capable of retracing their steps or renouncing the fatal acquisitions they had made, but, abusing the faculties that do them honor, labored merely to their own ruin and brought themselves to the brink of destruction.
"Astonished at the novelty of his own ills, both rich and miserable, he longs to flee from the riches, and hates what he had just been praying for." (Ovid, Metamorphoses xi, 127.)

It is impossible that men should not at length have reflected on so wretched a situation, and on the calamities that overwhelmed them. The rich, in particular, must have felt how much they suffered by a constant state of war, of which they bore all the expense, and in which, though all risked their lives, they alone risked their property. Besides, however speciously they might disguise their usurpations, they knew they were founded on precarious and false titles, so that if others took from them by force what they themselves had gained by force, they would have no reason to complain. Even those who had been enriched by their own industry could hardly base their proprietorship on better claims. It was in vain to repeat: "I built this well; I gained this spot by my industry." "Who gave you your standing?" it might be answered. "And what right have you to demand payment of us for doing what we never asked you to do? Do you not know that countless others of your fellow creatures are starving for want of what you have too much of? You ought to have had the express and universal consent of mankind before appropriating more of the common subsistence than you needed for your own maintenance." Destitute of valid reasons to justify himself, and of sufficient strength to defend himself; able to crush individuals with ease, but easily crushed himself by a troop of bandits; one against all, and incapable, on account of mutual jealousy, of joining with his equals against numerous enemies united by the common hope of plunder—the rich man, thus urged by necessity, conceived at length the most profound plan that ever entered the human mind. This was to employ in his favor the very forces of those who attacked him, to make allies of his adversaries, to inspire them with different maxims, and to give them other institutions as favorable to himself as the law of nature was unfavorable.

With this in view, after pointing out to his neighbors the horror of a situation that armed every man against the rest, and made their possessions as burdensome as their needs, in which no safety could be expected either in riches or in poverty, he readily devised plausible arguments to bring them around to his design. "Let us join together," he said, "to protect the weak from oppression, to restrain the ambitious, and to secure for every man the possession of what belongs to him. Let us institute rules of justice and peace to which all without exception are bound to conform—rules that may in some measure make up for the caprices of fortune, by subjecting equally the powerful and the weak to the observance of reciprocal obligations. Let us, in a word, instead of turning our forces against ourselves, collect them in a supreme power that may govern us by wise laws, protect and defend all the members of the association, repel their common enemies, and maintain eternal harmony among us."

Far fewer words to this purpose would have been enough to impose on men so barbarous and easily seduced, especially since they had too many disputes among themselves to do without arbitrators, and too much ambition and avarice to go long without masters. All ran headlong to their chains, in the hope of securing their liberty; for they had just enough wit to perceive the advantages of political institutions, but not enough experience to foresee the dangers. The most capable of foreseeing the dangers were the very ones who expected to benefit from them; and even the most prudent judged it not inexpedient to sacrifice one part of their freedom to secure the rest, just as a wounded man has his arm cut off to save the rest of his body.

Such was, or may well have been, the origin of society and laws, which laid new fetters on the poor and gave new powers to the rich; which irretrievably destroyed natural liberty, eternally fixed the law of property and inequality, converted clever usurpation into an unalterable right, and, for the advantage of a few ambitious individuals, subjected all mankind to perpetual labor, slavery, and wretchedness. It is easy to see how the establishment of one community made the establishment of all the others necessary, and how, in order to make head against united forces, the rest of mankind had to unite in turn. Societies soon multiplied and spread across the face of the earth until hardly a corner of the world was left in which a man could escape the yoke, and withdraw his head from beneath the sword which he saw perpetually hanging over him by a thread. Civil right having thus become the common rule among the members of each community, the law of nature retained its place only between different communities, where, under the name of the right of nations, it was qualified by certain tacit conventions in order to make commerce practicable and to serve as a substitute for natural compassion—which lost, when applied to societies, almost all the influence it had had over individuals, and survived no longer except in some great cosmopolitan spirits who, breaking down the imaginary barriers that separate different peoples, follow the example of our Sovereign Creator, and include the whole human race in their benevolence.

But political bodies, remaining thus in a state of nature among themselves, soon experienced the inconveniences that had compelled individuals to leave it. Indeed, this state became even more fatal to these great bodies than it had been to the individuals of whom they were composed. From this arose national wars, battles, murders, and reprisals—which shock nature and outrage reason—together with all those horrible prejudices that classify, among the virtues, the honor of shedding human blood. The most distinguished men learned from this to regard cutting one another's throats as a duty; eventually men massacred their fellow creatures by the thousands without so much as knowing why, and committed more murders in a single day's fighting, and more violent outrages in the sack of a single town, than were committed in the state of nature during whole ages over the whole earth. Such were the first effects we can see to have followed the division of mankind into different communities. But let us return to their institutions.

I know that some writers have given other explanations of the origin of political societies, such as the conquest of the powerful, or the association of the weak. It is, indeed, indifferent to my argument which of these causes we choose. The one I have just laid down, however, appears to me the most natural for the following reasons. First: because, in the first case, the right of conquest, being no right in itself, could not serve as the foundation on which to build any other; the victor and the vanquished people still remained, with respect to each other, in the state of war, unless the vanquished, restored to the full possession of their liberty, voluntarily made the victor their chief. For until then, whatever capitulation may have been made, being founded on violence and therefore null and void in itself, there could not on this hypothesis have been either a real society or a body politic, or any law other than that of the strongest. Secondly: because the words strong and weak are, in the second case, ambiguous; for in the interval between the establishment of a right of property, or prior occupancy, and that of political government, the meaning of these words is better expressed by the terms rich and poor, since, in fact, before the institution of laws, men had no other way of reducing their equals to submission than by attacking their goods, or making over some of their own to them. Thirdly: because, as the poor had nothing but their freedom to lose, it would have been in the highest degree absurd for them to resign voluntarily the only good they still enjoyed without getting anything in exchange; whereas the rich, having feelings, if I may put it so, in every part of their possessions, were much easier to harm, and so it was more necessary for them to take precautions against it. And, in short, because it is more reasonable to suppose that a thing was invented by those to whom it would be of service, than by those whom it must have harmed.

Government had, in its infancy, no regular and constant form. The want of experience and philosophy prevented men from seeing any but present inconveniences, and they only thought of providing against others as they presented themselves. In spite of the efforts of the wisest legislators, the political state remained imperfect, because it was little more than the work of chance; and as it had begun ill, though time revealed its defects and suggested remedies, the original faults were never repaired. It was continually being patched up, when the first task should have been to clear the site and remove all the old materials, as Lycurgus did at Sparta, if a stable and lasting edifice was to be erected. Society consisted at first merely of a few general conventions, which every member bound himself to observe; and for the performance of these covenants the whole body went security to each individual. Experience alone could show the weakness of such a constitution, and how easily it could be infringed with impunity, given the difficulty of convicting men of faults where the public alone was to be witness and judge. The laws could not but be evaded in many ways; disorders and inconveniences could not but multiply continually, until it became necessary to commit the dangerous trust of public authority to private persons, and to entrust the care of enforcing obedience to the deliberations of the people to a magistrate. For to say that chiefs were chosen before the confederacy was formed, and that the administrators of the laws were there before the laws themselves, is too absurd a supposition to consider seriously.

It would be just as unreasonable to suppose that men at first threw themselves irretrievably and unconditionally into the arms of an absolute master, and that the first expedient which proud and unsubdued men hit upon for their common security was to run headlong into slavery. For what reason, in fact, did they take to themselves superiors, if not in order to be defended from oppression and to have protection for their lives, liberties, and properties, which are, so to speak, the constituent elements of their being? Now in the relations between man and man, the worst that can happen is for one to find himself at the mercy of another; and it would have been inconsistent with common sense to begin by bestowing on a chief the very things they wanted his help to preserve. What equivalent could he offer them for so great a right? And if he had presumed to demand it under the pretext of defending them, would he not have received the answer recorded in the fable: "What more can the enemy do to us?" It is therefore beyond dispute, and indeed the fundamental maxim of all political right, that peoples have set up chiefs to protect their liberty, not to enslave them. "If we have a prince," said Pliny to Trajan, "it is to save us from having a master."

Politicians indulge in the same sophistry about the love of liberty as philosophers do about the state of nature. They judge, by what they see, of very different things they have not seen, and attribute to man a natural propensity to servitude because the slaves within their observation are seen to bear the yoke with patience. They fail to reflect that with liberty it is as it is with innocence and virtue: their value is known only to those who possess them, and the taste for them is lost when they themselves are lost. "I know the charms of your country," said Brasidas to a Persian satrap who was comparing the life at Sparta with that at Persepolis, "but you cannot know the pleasures of mine."

An unbroken horse erects his mane, paws the ground, and starts back impetuously at the sight of the bridle, while one which is properly trained patiently suffers even whip and spur. So savage man will not bend his neck to the yoke to which civilized man submits without a murmur, but prefers the most turbulent state of liberty to the most peaceful slavery. We cannot, therefore, from the servility of nations already enslaved, judge of the natural disposition of mankind for or against slavery; we should go by the prodigious efforts of every free people to save itself from oppression. I know that the former are forever holding forth in praise of the tranquility they enjoy in their chains, and that they call a state of wretched servitude a state of peace—"the most wretched slavery they call peace" (Tacitus, Histories iv, 17). But when I see the latter sacrificing pleasure, peace, wealth, power, and life itself to the preservation of that one treasure so disdained by those who have lost it; when I see free-born animals dash their brains out against the bars of their cage, from an innate impatience with captivity; when I behold numbers of naked savages who despise European pleasures, braving hunger, fire, the sword, and death to preserve nothing but their independence—I feel that it is not for slaves to argue about liberty.

With regard to paternal authority, from which some writers have derived absolute government and all society, it is enough, without going back to the contrary arguments of Locke and Sidney, to note that nothing on earth could be further from the ferocious spirit of despotism than the mildness of that authority, which looks more to the advantage of him who obeys than to that of him who commands; that by the law of nature, the father is the child's master no longer than his help is necessary; that from that time they are both equal, the son being perfectly independent of the father and owing him only respect, not obedience. For gratitude is a duty that ought to be paid, but not a right to be exacted. Instead of saying that civil society is derived from paternal authority, we ought to say rather that the latter derives its principal force from the former. No individual was ever acknowledged as the father of many until his sons and daughters settled around him. The goods of the father, of which he is really the master, are the ties that keep his children in dependence, and he may bestow on them, if he pleases, no share of his property unless they merit it by constant deference to his will. But the subjects of an arbitrary despot are so far from having any like favor to expect from their chief that they themselves and everything they possess are his property—or at least are considered by him as such—so that they are forced to receive, as a favor, the little of their own he is pleased to leave them. When he despoils them, he does but justice; and mercy, in that he permits them to live.

By proceeding thus to test fact by right, we should discover as little reason as truth in the voluntary establishment of tyranny. It would also be no easy matter to prove the validity of a contract binding on only one of the parties, where all the risk is on one side and none on the other—so that no one could suffer but he who bound himself. This hateful system is indeed, even in modern times, very far from being that of wise and good monarchs, especially the kings of France, as may be seen from several passages in their edicts; particularly from the following passage in a celebrated edict published in 1667 in the name and by order of Louis XIV.

"Let it not, therefore, be said that the Sovereign is not subject to the laws of his State, since the contrary is a true proposition of the right of nations, which flattery has sometimes attacked but good princes have always defended as the tutelary divinity of their dominions. How much more legitimate is it to say with the wise Plato, that the perfect felicity of a kingdom consists in the obedience of subjects to their prince, and of the prince to the laws, and in the laws being just and constantly directed to the public good!" (Of the Rights of the Most Christian Queen over various States of the Monarchy of Spain, 1667.)

I will not stay here to inquire whether, since liberty is the noblest faculty of man, it is not degrading our very nature, reducing ourselves to the level of the brutes that are mere slaves of instinct, and even an affront to the Author of our being, to renounce without reserve the most precious of all His gifts, and to bow to the necessity of committing all the crimes He has forbidden, merely to gratify a mad or cruel master; or whether this sublime craftsman ought not to be less angered at seeing His workmanship entirely destroyed than thus dishonored. I will waive (if my opponents please) the authority of Barbeyrac, who, following Locke, roundly declares that no man can so far sell his liberty as to submit to an arbitrary power that may use him as it likes. For, he adds, this would be to sell his own life, of which he is not master. I will ask only what right those who were not afraid to debase themselves in this way could have to subject their posterity to the same ignominy, and to renounce for them those blessings they do not owe to the liberality of their progenitors, and without which life itself must be a burden to all who are worthy of it.

Pufendorf says that we may divest ourselves of our liberty in favor of other men, just as we transfer our property from one to another by contracts and agreements. But this seems a very weak argument. For in the first place, the property I give up becomes entirely foreign to me, and I cannot suffer from the abuse of it; but it very nearly concerns me that my liberty should not be abused, and I cannot, without incurring the guilt of the crimes I may be compelled to commit, expose myself to becoming an instrument of crime. Besides, the right of property being only a convention of human institution, men may dispose of what they possess as they please; but this is not the case with the essential gifts of nature, such as life and liberty, which every man is permitted to enjoy, and of which it is at least doubtful whether anyone has a right to divest themselves. By giving up the one, we degrade our being; by giving up the other, we do our best to annul it; and since no temporal good can compensate us for the loss of either, it would be an offense against both reason and nature to renounce them at any price whatsoever. But even if we could transfer our liberty as we do our property, there would be a great difference with regard to the children, who enjoy the father's substance only by the transmission of his right; whereas, liberty being a gift they hold from nature as men, their parents have no right whatsoever to deprive them of it. So just as to establish slavery it was necessary to do violence to nature, in order to perpetuate such a right, nature would have to be changed. Jurists, who have gravely determined that the child of a slave comes into the world a slave, have decided, in other words, that a man shall come into the world not a man.

I regard it, then, as certain that government did not begin with arbitrary power, but that this is the depravation, the extreme term, of government, and brings it back, finally, to just the law of the strongest, which it was originally designed to remedy. Even supposing it had begun in this manner, such power, being in itself illegitimate, could not have served as a basis for the laws of society, nor, consequently, for the inequality they instituted.

Without entering for now into the investigations still to be made into the nature of the fundamental compact underlying all government, I content myself with adopting the common opinion concerning it, and regard the establishment of the political body as a real contract between the people and the chiefs they have chosen—a contract by which both parties bind themselves to observe the laws therein expressed, which form the ties of their union. The people, having concentrated all their wills in one with respect to their social relations, the various articles in which this will is expressed become so many fundamental laws, binding on all the members of the state without exception. One of these articles regulates the choice and power of the magistrates appointed to watch over the execution of the rest. This power extends to everything that may maintain the constitution, without going so far as to alter it. It is accompanied by honors, in order to bring the laws and their administrators into respect. The ministers are also distinguished by personal prerogatives in order to compensate them for the cares and labor that good administration involves. The magistrate, for his part, binds himself to use the power entrusted to him only in conformity with the intention of his constituents, to maintain them all in the peaceable possession of what belongs to them, and to prefer on every occasion the public interest to his own.

Before experience had shown, or knowledge of the human heart enabled men to foresee, the unavoidable abuses of such a constitution, it must have appeared all the more excellent because those who were charged with the care of its preservation had themselves the most interest in it. For magistracy and the rights attaching to it being based solely on the fundamental laws, the magistrates would cease to be legitimate as soon as these ceased to exist; the people would no longer owe them obedience; and since not the magistrates but the laws are essential to the being of a state, the members of it would regain their right to their natural liberty.

If we reflect with even a little attention on this subject, we shall find new arguments to confirm this truth, and be convinced from the very nature of the contract that it cannot be irrevocable. For if there were no superior power capable of ensuring the fidelity of the contracting parties, or compelling them to perform their reciprocal engagements, the parties would be sole judges in their own cause, and each would always have a right to renounce the contract as soon as he found that the other had violated its terms, or that they no longer suited his convenience. It is on this principle that the right of abdication may possibly be founded. Now, if, as here, we consider only what is human in this institution, it is certain that, if the magistrate, who has all the power in his own hands and appropriates all the advantages of the contract for himself, has nonetheless a right to renounce his authority, the people, who suffer for all the faults of their chief, must have a much better right to renounce their dependence. But the terrible and innumerable quarrels and disorders that would necessarily arise from so dangerous a privilege show, more than anything else, how much human governments stood in need of a more solid basis than mere reason, and how expedient it was for the public tranquility that the divine will should interpose to invest the sovereign authority with a sacred and inviolable character, which might deprive subjects of the fatal right of disposing of it. If the world had received no other advantages from religion, this would be enough to impose on men the duty of adopting and cultivating it, abuses and all, since it has been the means of saving more blood than fanaticism has ever spilt. But let us follow the thread of our hypothesis.

The different forms of government owe their origin to the different degrees of inequality that existed among individuals at the time of their institution. If there happened to be any one man among them pre-eminent in power, virtue, riches, or personal influence, he became sole magistrate, and the state assumed the form of monarchy. If several, nearly equal in eminence, stood above the rest, they were elected jointly, and formed an aristocracy. Again, among a people who had deviated less from a state of nature, and between whose fortune or talents there was less disproportion, the supreme administration was retained in common, and a democracy was formed.
